paragraphs.text: Zhuangyuan Hong (状元红) is an oolong from the [Wuyi Mountains](wuyi-mountains:where-it-is), the range along the border of northern Fujian and Jiangxi, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1999. The bushes here grow on ledges and between rocks in the ravines, in thin soil that drains fast and under mist that settles on the slopes, and that ground is the reason the trade ties this tea so closely to the rock. [Oolong is traced to this area](fujian:history), and its making is said to have spread from here to Anxi, Guangdong and then Taiwan.

Like all [Wuyi rock tea](yancha:definition), it is [partly oxidised](oolong:definition): withered in the sun, cooled indoors, shaken and rested, fixed in a hot pan or drum, then twisted into long strips rather than rolled into balls. What sets it apart is the [charcoal roast](yancha:making), given in several rounds with rests of weeks or months between them, which dries the leaf so it keeps. After roasting the tea is rested again before it is drunk, and [the heavier the roast](yancha:roast-levels), the longer that rest.

brewing.text: Wuyi tea is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C, and about 5 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 120 ml gaiwan, a third to a half full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 5 to 20 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and good rock tea gives seven steeps or more. In a larger pot, use about 2 to 5 grams for 250 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

notice.text: Roast and stone fruit, a mineral, rocky texture and a long, sweet, mouth-watering finish. Light roast is bright and floral, medium roast fruity and rounded, full roast charcoal, wood and roasted nuts. Da Hong Pao is often floral, Rougui spicy with cinnamon, young Shui Xian sweet and smooth, and old-bush Shui Xian woody and mossy.
